supplements.citation: Idaho DHW About SNAP and Apply for SNAP consumer pages (healthandwelfare.idaho.gov); Idalink self-service portal (idalink.idaho.gov); IDAPA 16.03.04 ("Idaho Food Stamp Program")
supplements.heading: Idaho calls its program plainly "SNAP" on consumer pages — the administrative code's own title is the older "Idaho Food Stamp Program," and the self-service portal is Idalink
supplements.text: Idaho DHW's own consumer materials use the generic federal name "SNAP" (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program), noting it was "formerly known as Food Stamps" — this pack found no distinctive Idaho-specific program nickname the way California has "CalFresh" or Washington has "Basic Food." Idaho's underlying administrative code, however, still carries the program's older name in its own title: IDAPA 16.03.04, "Idaho Food Stamp Program" — the rule text itself consistently uses "Food Stamps" throughout rather than "SNAP," a naming lag between the state's formal rule and its own consumer-facing branding that this pack flags as worth knowing (a reader who finds the rule text directly should not conclude Idaho renamed or restructured the program). Idaho's current self-service application portal is Idalink (idalink.idaho.gov), which DHW describes as a single account covering SNAP, Medicaid, cash assistance, and child care assistance together. Applicants can also apply by phone or in person through DHW's toll-free line (1-877-456-1233) and nearest field office, or by mail, email (MyBenefits@dhw.idaho.gov), or fax (1-866-434-8278) to Self-Reliance Programs, PO Box 83720, Boise, ID 83720-0026. Idaho's SNAP program is administered directly and centrally by DHW's Self-Reliance Programs division — a state-administered program with no county-level policy authority, structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, North Carolina, Ohio, New Jersey, Tennessee, Indiana, Missouri, Maryland, Colorado, South Carolina, Alabama, Louisiana, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Utah, Iowa, and Arkansas packs, and distinct from county-administered states like CA, NY, MN, WI, and VA. An interview (face-to-face or by phone) is required with every application; households can be required to complete a written six-month or twelve-month "contact" between full recertifications, which waives the interview requirement for that check-in.

supplements.citation: Idaho DHW, Apply for SNAP consumer page (effective October 2025 monthly gross income limits by household size); IDAPA 16.03.04.532 (Gross Income Limit — elderly/disabled households exempt); IDAPA 16.03.04.178 (Categorically Eligible Households)
supplements.heading: Idaho does NOT run an elevated BBCE income ceiling — the gross-income limit is the plain federal 130% FPL figure for every non-categorically-eligible household
supplements.text: Unlike this roster's Nebraska (165% FPL for a scoped subset of households) and several other BBCE states with an elevated income ceiling above the federal baseline, Idaho DHW's own current Apply for SNAP page publishes ONE gross monthly income limit table, effective October 2025, matching the plain federal 130% FPL standard: $1,696 for a household of one, $2,292 (two), $2,888 (three), $3,483 (four), $4,079 (five), $4,675 (six), $5,271 (seven), $5,867 (eight), plus $596 for each additional member. These figures match, to the dollar, this roster's Nebraska pack's own confirmed 130% FPL figures for the same FFY2026 cycle — a useful independent cross-check that both packs are reading the same current federal cost-of-living update correctly. IDAPA 16.03.04.532 provides one meaningful state-administered exception: a household with an elderly or disabled member is EXEMPT from the gross income limit entirely (subject instead only to the net income limit, IDAPA 549, after deductions — net income must not exceed 100% FPL). Idaho also recognizes a narrower Categorical Eligibility (CE) pathway (IDAPA 178): households where every member receives or is authorized to receive TAFI, AABD, or SSI cash benefits are categorically eligible and the Department will NOT compute resource eligibility, gross income limits, or net income limits for them at all — a full waiver of all three financial tests, distinct from Idaho's Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility pathway, which raises the resource limit but does NOT waive the income tests (see asset-rule supplement for the resource-side distinction this pack flags as a flagship correction).

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.010.09 (Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility definition — BBCE households remain "subject to resource, gross, and net income eligibility standards"); IDAPA 16.03.04.305 (Resource Limit — $5,000 flat for BBCE households); Idaho DHW Apply for SNAP page ("For most households, resources must be under $5,000")
supplements.heading: FLAGSHIP CORRECTION: Idaho's BBCE does NOT waive the resource test — it RAISES the limit to a flat $5,000, contradicting a widely-repeated secondary-source claim that Idaho BBCE households face "no resource limit"
supplements.text: This pack found a genuine, consequential correction to make here, one that appeared directly in this pack's own preliminary web-search synthesis before primary-source verification caught it: multiple aggregator/secondary sources describe Idaho as having "adopted BBCE with no resource limit," concluding a car's value "does not affect SNAP eligibility" for any Idaho household. Idaho's own administrative code says the opposite in as many words. IDAPA 16.03.04.010.09 defines Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility precisely: "If a participant meets the eligibility requirements found in 7 CFR Section 273.2(j)(2) and also all other Food Stamp eligibility criteria, then the participant is eligible for Food Stamps. Participants who are eligible under this definition are ALSO SUBJECT TO resource, gross, and net income eligibility standards" (emphasis this pack's own, to flag the operative clause precisely). IDAPA 16.03.04.305 then states that operative resource standard directly: "The Food Stamp resource limit is five thousand dollars ($5,000) for Broad-Based Categorically Eligible households. Households that do not meet the requirements for Broad-Based Categorical Eligibility are subject to resource limits published by [FNS]" — i.e., the plain federal baseline ($3,000 general, $4,500 elderly/disabled, per the current FFY2026 FNS-published figures this roster's other packs have independently confirmed). This pack independently cross-checked the $5,000 figure against DHW's own separate, plain-language Apply for SNAP consumer page, which states without qualification: "For most households, resources must be under $5,000 to qualify for SNAP. Resources include... Cash, Bank accounts, Stocks and bonds, Property, Household and recreational vehicles" — DHW's own consumer page listing vehicles among counted resource TYPES is itself a second, independent contradiction of the "car value doesn't matter" secondary-source claim. This pack reads Idaho's structure as: a genuine, real, ELEVATED resource limit ($5,000, above the federal baseline) for the broad BBCE-eligible population, distinct from Idaho's narrower Categorical Eligibility (CE) pathway (TAFI/AABD/SSI recipients, IDAPA 178), which IS a full waiver of the resource test (along with gross and net income) — structurally similar, in the SHAPE of the BBCE-vs-CE distinction, to this roster's Nebraska ERP-vs-CE finding, though Idaho's BBCE dollar figure ($5,000 flat, no elderly/disabled tier distinction) is simpler than Nebraska's three-tier ($4,500/$3,000/$25,000) structure. IDAPA 16.03.04.334 (Vehicles) further specifies that vehicles used PRIMARILY for recreational purposes count toward the resource limit, while other vehicles' values are counted per 7 CFR 273's federal methodology — this pack did not find an Idaho-specific per-vehicle dollar exclusion figure beyond the federal default and flags this as an area to re-verify directly against IDAPA 16.03.04.334's full subsection text before stating a specific vehicle-exclusion dollar amount.

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.287 (Ineligibility for a Felony Conviction for Possession, Use, or Distribution of a Controlled Substance) — eligible while complying with the terms of a withheld judgment, probation, or parole; ineligible if not complying
supplements.heading: Idaho runs a MODIFIED drug-felony ban conditioned on compliance with sentencing terms — no treatment-program requirement, a genuine structural difference from Nebraska's modified-ban mechanism
supplements.text: 21 U.S.C. § 862a(a)(2) sets a federal default: anyone convicted of a state or federal felony for possessing, using, or distributing a controlled substance is permanently ineligible for SNAP unless a state opts out or modifies the ban under § 862a(d)(1). Idaho has modified, not fully opted out of, the federal ban. IDAPA 16.03.04.287 states plainly: "Individuals convicted under federal or state law of a felony involving the possession, use, or distribution of a controlled substance can receive Food Stamps when they comply with the terms of a withheld judgment, probation, or parole. Controlled substance felons who are NOT complying with the terms of a withheld judgment, probation, or parole are not eligible for Food Stamps." This pack flags a genuine structural difference worth naming precisely against this roster's most recently built comparison state, Nebraska: Nebraska's modified ban (Neb. Rev. Stat. § 68-1017.02(1)(b)) is scoped by CONVICTION COUNT (permanent ineligibility only for three-or-more possession/use felonies or any sale/distribution felony) and conditions continued eligibility for lesser convictions on participation in a substance-abuse TREATMENT PROGRAM. Idaho's rule instead conditions eligibility on ONGOING COMPLIANCE WITH SENTENCING TERMS (a withheld judgment, probation, or parole) — no explicit treatment-program requirement appears in IDAPA 16.03.04.287's text, and no conviction-count threshold (a single controlled-substance felony conviction, regardless of severity, triggers the compliance condition under Idaho's rule as this pack reads it). This pack did not find any Idaho legislative activity in the 2025-2026 session analogous to Nebraska's LB319 (a bill that would have replaced the modified ban with a broader eligibility rule) — Idaho's IDAPA 16.03.04.287 read as this pack's most current, unqualified, primary-source text of the state's operative policy.

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.251-258 (ABAWD Work Requirement, dated 7-1-24 — PRE-OBBBA text, now superseded on age range and exemption scope by federal law); OBBBA (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, effective 10/20/2025 nationally) raised the ABAWD age ceiling to 64 and removed veteran/homeless/foster-youth exemptions nationwide
supplements.heading: FRESHNESS FLAG: Idaho's own published IDAPA 16.03.04 ABAWD text is now STALE relative to OBBBA — it still shows the pre-OBBBA age range (18-53/55) and the pre-OBBBA exemption list (veterans, homeless individuals, foster youth) that federal law removed nationwide effective October 20, 2025
supplements.text: An able-bodied adult without dependents (ABAWD) is limited to three countable months of SNAP within a 36-month period absent 80 hours/month of a qualifying work activity (JSAP, Idaho's own work-program name, or another recognized work program) or an exemption. This pack found IDAPA 16.03.04.257's own text, dated 7-1-24 (i.e., last formally updated before the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act), states the ABAWD age exemption as "Persons under eighteen (18) and fifty-three (53) years old or older. Beginning October 1, 2024, the age limit increases to fifty-five (55)" — and separately exempts veterans ("regardless of the reason for discharge or release"), homeless individuals, and (implicitly, under the same pre-OBBBA federal framework) individuals aging out of foster care. This pack flags plainly: this text is NOW SUPERSEDED by federal law, not a current statement of Idaho's operative ABAWD age range or exemption list. OBBBA raised the nationwide ABAWD age ceiling to 64 (from the 54/55 range IDAPA 16.03.04.257 still shows) and REMOVED the veteran, homeless, and foster-youth discretionary exemption categories nationwide, effective October 20, 2025 — this pack did not find evidence Idaho's own IDAPA rule text has been formally amended to reflect either change as of this pack's fetch date, a genuine administrative-code lag this pack found directly by reading the rule's own effective-date stamp rather than assuming a rule text is automatically current just because it is the state's own official code. An Idaho SNAP applicant or caseworker relying on IDAPA 16.03.04.257's literal text alone would be applying an outdated age range and an exemption list that includes three categories federal law removed. Separately, IDAPA 16.03.04.251.05 ("Residents of High Unemployment Areas") preserves a state-administered mechanism for county-level ABAWD relief where the Department identifies high unemployment or job scarcity — this pack found secondary-source corroboration (not a directly-fetched, dated current-waiver list) that Idaho does NOT currently maintain an active statewide or area-wide ABAWD waiver, meaning all counties are, as of this pack's fetch date, presumed subject to the standard three-month time limit absent an individual exemption — but flags this specific current-waiver-status claim as secondary-source-corroborated only, not independently confirmed against a dated USDA FNS active-waiver list for Idaho specifically, see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: Idaho DHW, About SNAP consumer page ("What You Cannot Buy with SNAP" lists "Hot, prepared foods meant to be eaten right away" with no restaurant/RMP carve-out mentioned)
supplements.heading: Idaho does NOT currently operate a Restaurant Meals Program
supplements.text: The Restaurant Meals Program (RMP) is a state OPTION under 7 CFR § 274.7(g) letting elderly (60+), disabled, and homeless SNAP recipients buy prepared, hot meals from authorized restaurants with EBT year-round. Idaho DHW's own About SNAP page lists "Hot, prepared foods meant to be eaten right away" among the items SNAP benefits cannot purchase, with no exception or carve-out mentioned for elderly, disabled, or homeless households — this pack found no evidence anywhere in its Idaho research (DHW's own consumer materials, IDAPA 16.03.04's full text, or USDA's current RMP participation list) that Idaho operates a Restaurant Meals Program. This pack's operative answer for an Idaho applicant today is that Idaho does NOT currently offer a Restaurant Meals Program.

supplements.citation: Idaho DHW, SNAP Retailer Information Page / Candy and Soda Restrictions (effective 2/15/2026, Idaho House Bill 109, no medical exemptions, page dated 4/27/2026); Aragon et al. v. Rollins et al., 1:26-cv-00861 (D.D.C.), order dated June 22, 2026, vacating Colorado's, Iowa's, Nebraska's, Tennessee's, and West Virginia's food-restriction waivers specifically — Idaho was not a party and was not vacated
supplements.heading: TIME-SENSITIVE FLAGSHIP FINDING: unlike Nebraska's soda/energy-drink waiver (vacated by a federal court in June 2026), Idaho's candy-and-soda restriction remains ACTIVE — Idaho was not a party to the lawsuit that struck down five other states' waivers
supplements.text: This pack found and flags a genuinely important contrast with this roster's Nebraska pack, built immediately prior: Nebraska's SNAP soda/energy-drink purchase restriction was approved, took effect January 1, 2026, and was then VACATED by a federal court on June 22, 2026 in Aragon et al. v. Rollins et al. (D.D.C.). A reader encountering that finding first could reasonably — but WRONGLY — assume every state's similar food-restriction waiver met the same fate. Idaho's did not. Idaho DHW requested, and USDA approved, a candy-and-soda purchase restriction under Idaho House Bill 109, with an implementation date USDA approved moving from January 1, 2026 to February 15, 2026 (approved December 12, 2025). This pack fetched Idaho DHW's own retailer-facing Candy and Soda Restrictions page directly and found it dated April 27, 2026 — more than FIVE WEEKS AFTER the June 22, 2026 Aragon v. Rollins order — describing the restriction as actively in force, with the explicit statement "There are no medical exemptions to this restriction. Candy and soda cannot be purchased with SNAP benefits, regardless of medical need," and no mention anywhere on the page of a court order, vacatur, or rollback. This pack cross-checked this against Covington & Burling LLP's own legal-analysis summary of the Aragon v. Rollins order, which names the SPECIFIC states whose waivers the court vacated: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee, and West Virginia. Idaho is not on that list, and secondary reporting this pack found corroborates Idaho state officials asserting the ruling does not apply to Idaho's restriction because Idaho was not a party to that suit — a position consistent with (though not itself proof of) the court's own order being scoped to the specific plaintiff states rather than a nationwide vacatur of every state's food-restriction waiver. "Candy" and "soda" are defined under Idaho House Bill 109's own terms: candy is a sugar/honey/artificial-sweetener preparation combined with chocolate, fruit, nuts, or flavorings in confection form, EXCLUDING any preparation containing flour and requiring no refrigeration; soda is any nonalcoholic sweetened beverage EXCLUDING beverages containing milk/milk substitutes, beverages that are more than 50% vegetable or fruit juice by volume, and beverages requiring preparation before consumption (powders, concentrates). This pack's operative answer for an Idaho SNAP applicant is that candy and soda, as Idaho's own definitions describe them, are NOT currently purchasable with SNAP benefits — a live, actively-enforced restriction distinct from Nebraska's vacated one, and this pack flags this as the kind of fact most likely to be misapplied by a reader (or a future pack-builder) generalizing from Nebraska's outcome.

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.010-011 (utility allowance definitions: SUA, LUA, MUA, TUA); IDAPA 16.03.04.543 (Utility Allowances — four-tier structure, qualifying criteria); IDAPA 16.03.04.533.07 (Excess Shelter Expense Deduction — over 50% of income after deductions)
supplements.heading: Idaho runs a FOUR-tier utility-allowance system (SUA/LUA/MUA/TUA) — structurally matching this roster's Nebraska pack's own four-tier finding, though this pack could NOT confirm Idaho's current dollar figures from a directly-fetched, dated DHW source
supplements.text: IDAPA 16.03.04.543 states the shelter deduction is computed using one of four utility allowances — SUA, LUA, MUA, or TUA — not prorated, and a household is limited to one SUA. This pack read each definition directly: the Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) applies to a household with a primary heating or cooling cost billed separately from rent/mortgage; the Limited Utility Allowance (LUA) applies to a household billed for more than one utility that is NOT for heating or cooling (electricity/fuel for non-heating purposes, water, sewage, well/septic maintenance, telephone, garbage/trash); the Minimum Utility Allowance (MUA) applies to a household billed for exactly one utility that is not heating, cooling, or telephone; and the Telephone Utility Allowance (TUA) applies to a household billed for telephone service with no other verified utility expense. This pack flags this as a genuine structural match — not merely a coincidental similarity — to this roster's Nebraska pack's own four-tier finding (SUA/LUA/OUA/Telephone Allowance): both states split the typical three-tier structure (most other states in this roster use SUA/Limited/Telephone-only) into a distinct "two-or-more non-heating utilities" tier and a separate "exactly-one non-heating, non-phone utility" tier, rather than treating those as the same tier. This pack could NOT, however, locate Idaho's CURRENT dollar figures for SUA, LUA, MUA, or TUA from a directly-fetched, dated DHW source the way this roster's Nebraska pack located Nebraska's — IDAPA 16.03.04's own rule text defines the four allowances by qualifying criteria only and does not itself state dollar amounts (Idaho, like several states in this roster, appears to publish the actual current dollar figures in a separate internal eligibility manual or periodic update this pack's fetch window did not converge on). This pack DISCLOSES this as a genuine, unresolved sourcing gap rather than reusing a secondary-source figure it could not verify — see freshness.json. The Excess Shelter Expense Deduction (IDAPA 16.03.04.533.07) is capped, for households without an elderly/disabled member, at the monthly shelter cost exceeding 50% of income after all other deductions (federal law exempts elderly/disabled households from any excess-shelter cap); this pack found a secondary-source-corroborated $744 maximum shelter deduction figure matching this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Kentucky, and Louisiana packs' own confirmed current FFY2026 figure, but flags this specific dollar amount as secondary-source-corroborated only for Idaho, not directly fetched from a dated DHW table, see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.535 (Medical Expenses — Standard Medical Expense (SME) deduction available to elderly/disabled households with verified medical expenses over $35/month, as an alternative to an actual-expense deduction)
supplements.heading: Idaho offers a flat Standard Medical Expense (SME) shortcut as an ALTERNATIVE to actual-expense verification — a genuine structural match to this roster's Kentucky/Louisiana/South Carolina/Missouri/Colorado/Alabama flat-shortcut camp, distinct from Nebraska's actual-expense-only mechanism
supplements.text: IDAPA 16.03.04.535 states that elderly or disabled household members with medical expenses exceeding $35/month are allowed a Standard Medical Expense (SME) deduction, and gives the household a genuine CHOICE: "Households with medical expenses that exceed the monthly SME may either verify the minimum amount to receive the SME or request and verify excess costs to receive an actual expense deduction." This pack reads Idaho's mechanism as placing it in the SAME structural camp as this roster's Kentucky ($137), Louisiana ($161), South Carolina ($175), Missouri ($135), Colorado ($165), and Alabama ($185) packs — a flat-figure shortcut available without full itemized verification — rather than this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut, Maryland, and Indiana packs' actual-expense-only mechanism (no flat shortcut at all). This pack found a specific dollar figure, $144, repeated across several secondary sources for Idaho's current SME amount, but flags this figure explicitly as SECONDARY-SOURCE-CORROBORATED ONLY — this pack's own direct fetch of IDAPA 16.03.04.535 confirmed the SME MECHANISM (the $35 threshold and the choice between SME and actual-expense verification) but the rule text itself does not state the current SME dollar amount, deferring it to a DHW-published standard this pack's fetch window did not locate directly. Re-verify the $144 figure against DHW's own current published standard before treating it as a confirmed hard fact — see freshness.json.

supplements.citation: IDAPA 16.03.04.120 (Household Interviews — frequency: every 24 months for households certified for 24 months, every 12 months for all other households); IDAPA 16.03.04's Extended Certification Household (EC) definition (all elderly/disabled, no earned income)
supplements.heading: Idaho ties its INTERVIEW frequency directly to certification-period length — 24-month interview cadence for 24-month-certified households, 12 months for everyone else — but this pack could not confirm the underlying certification-period LENGTHS by household category from a single directly-fetched section
supplements.text: IDAPA 16.03.04.120 states Idaho's interview-frequency rule precisely: an interview (face-to-face or telephone) is required at least once every twenty-four (24) months for households certified for a twenty-four (24) month period, and every twelve (12) months for all other households. IDAPA 16.03.04 separately defines an Extended Certification Household (EC) as "a household in which all members are elderly or disabled, and no one has earned income" — this pack reads the EC designation as the category most likely tied to the longer, 24-month certification cadence (structurally similar to this roster's Nebraska, Connecticut ESAP, and Kentucky ESAP packs' own elderly/disabled long-certification findings), but flags this inference explicitly: this pack's fetch of IDAPA 16.03.04 did not locate a single, explicit section stating "EC households receive a 24-month certification period" in as many words — Section 120 states the interview-frequency RULE (which certainly implies EC households are among those eligible for a 24-month certification), but the certification-PERIOD-ASSIGNMENT rule itself (which specific household categories receive which specific period length) sits in a different part of the code this pack's fetch window did not fully resolve. Idaho also recognizes a "six-month or twelve-month contact" — a written, interview-waived check-in between full recertifications — appearing throughout the rule's household-composition, income-change, and work-registration sections. Treat the EC-household-to-24-month-certification link as a reasonable but not fully section-confirmed inference, and re-verify against IDAPA 16.03.04's certification-period-assignment section directly before treating it as a hard fact in a high-stakes context.
